ApprovePolicyRequest.description:
Approve REUSE of the decision this case already made.

Separate from resolving the case, deliberately: a one-time resolution is
never auto-promoted into a reusable rule. The scope is the case's own
vendor and effect; only the validity window is chosen here.

Both shapes the real callers send: the verify suites post
{valid_from, valid_to} directly, and the case screen posts the same
fields inside the C03 envelope's `payload` (see
`EnvelopeTolerantRequest`). Before the flattening, the envelope form was
answered "valid_from: Field required" to a reviewer who had chosen a
window, so the control on the case screen could not be used at all.
ApprovePolicyRequest.title: ApprovePolicyRequest

ApprovePolicyVersionResult.description: C03 command result: the authoritative state, plus the whole record.
ApprovePolicyVersionResult.title: ApprovePolicyVersionResult

ApproveRequest.description:
Both shapes the real callers send (see `EnvelopeTolerantRequest`).

The last four fields are lane B's `ApprovePayoutPayload` (draft Q39),
which is what the approval screen puts inside the envelope's `payload`.
They are echoes of what the approver was shown, so the server refuses
an approval that no longer matches any of them -- and because extras
are forbidden, a field the UI starts sending that the server does not
know is a loud 422 rather than a silently discarded consent echo.
ApproveRequest.title: ApproveRequest

ResolveCaseRequest.description:
Two accepted shapes for one command.

The original shape states the rate directly: `decision` of
approve/edit/reject plus `commission_bps`. Scripts and the verify suites
use it and it is unchanged.

The reviewer-facing shape names the option instead:
`decision: "ACCEPT_OPTION" | "REJECT"` with `option_id`, and binds the
decision to what the reviewer actually saw via `evidence_hash` and
`expected_version`. The rate then comes from the case's own evidence, so
the client never supplies the number that decides money.
ResolveCaseRequest.title: ResolveCaseRequest

The C05 business configuration: how this festival charges and pays.

The finance posting config carries the versioned, stored part (timezone,
the 9 AM / 10 AM times, the forecast horizon, the tax configuration). The
rest -- the default terms a vendor falls back to and the payout controls --

get.description:
Match groups, oldest first, one page at a time.

This route previously took no `limit` and returned every matching row,
each one costing its own members query. On the real festival that is
201,035 groups: ~220 MB of JSON and ~32 seconds, which reads as a screen
stuck on "loading" rather than as a slow response. A reconciliation
database only grows, so an unbounded list here can never be safe.

Paging is keyset, not OFFSET: `cursor` is the id of the last group on the
previous page and the scan resumes after that row's (created_at, id). An
OFFSET page would re-scan everything before it and would also skip or
repeat rows when a new run inserts groups mid-read, which is exactly what
happens here while a close is running.

`status` accepts either spelling (see _GROUP_STATUSES) and refuses an
unknown one rather than returning an unfiltered page, and
`business_date` is honoured -- the screen sent both already.

The response stays a bare array, as it was, so existing callers are
unaffected; the client treats a bare array as one unpaged page. The next
page is requested with `cursor=<id of the last item>`.

get.description:
Every report that can be produced for this festival, newest basis first.

`next_cursor` is always null: there are three kinds, not a stream of
reports, so the envelope keeps the shape every other list uses without
pretending to page.
One report, resolved from an id that states its own inputs.

Settlements, oldest first, one page at a time, without line items.

This took no `limit` and returned every matching row with its line items
embedded: 640 rows and 129 MB of JSON on the real festival, because each
row's line items carry a source_ref per contributing payment and match
group. The size, not the query, was what made the screen slow.

Paging is keyset rather than OFFSET, for the same reason as the match-group
list: a close run inserting settlements mid-read must not make a page skip
or repeat rows. `cursor` is the id of the last row on the previous page.

`status` is accepted alongside the original `status_` so the name the
client sends actually binds.

get.description:
TICKET section 7. Quote amounts come from the imported `supplier_quotes`
rows (demo-clock-gated by `available_at <= as_of`); the cash-impact
baseline and supplier history are read directly from the fixture's
cash_inputs.json/historical_contracts.json -- a labelled synthetic
comparison, never written to cash_pools/opening_balances/the journal.
Selection stays undecided here: no winner field, no aggregate score.

`as_of` is a full timezone-aware instant (not a bare date): a quote
available at 09:00 on its release day must not leak into a comparison
made at, say, 08:00 that same day.

cursor is an opaque decimal offset over a stable (name, id) order, and

and always answer even if the database is unreachable, so orchestrators
can distinguish 'process is wedged' from 'dependency is down'.
